cards.intuition: Cut the ranking after k results and temporarily treat that prefix as an unordered retrieved set. Precision asks how clean the prefix is; recall asks how much of the known relevant set it captured.
cards.formula: P@k = relevant in top-k / k; R@k = relevant in top-k / total relevant
cards.topic: Precision@k and Recall@k: What Ranking Changes

cards.concept: What are cutoff metrics blind to?
cards.intuition: They see whether a result crossed the top-k boundary but not where it sits inside the prefix. Swapping a relevant rank-1 result with a rank-k result leaves both metrics unchanged.
cards.formula: same top-k membership → same P@k and R@k
cards.topic: Precision@k and Recall@k: What Ranking Changes

cards.concept: How should k match the retrieval consumer?
cards.intuition: Measure the prefix the next actor can actually use. A five-chunk prompt needs top-5 quality, while a reranker candidate stage needs high recall at its much deeper input limit.
cards.topic: Precision@k and Recall@k: What Ranking Changes

cards.concept: Why can P@k have a ceiling below 1?
cards.intuition: If only three documents are relevant, a ten-slot prefix can contain at most three relevant results. The query's scarcity, not the ranker's quality, caps P@10 at 0.3.
cards.topic: Precision@k and Recall@k: What Ranking Changes

cards.intuition: Walk the ranking and record precision whenever a relevant result appears, then average those values over all relevant documents. Early clean hits contribute more than late diluted hits.
cards.formula: AP = (1/R) × sum of P@rank(d) over relevant d; missed relevant documents contribute 0

cards.concept: Why does AP resemble area under a precision-recall curve?
cards.intuition: Each relevant hit raises recall by exactly 1/R. Multiplying each sampled precision by that equal recall step forms a Riemann sum over recall.
cards.formula: AP ≈ integral of precision with respect to recall

cards.intuition: MAP gives every evaluable query one vote by averaging per-query AP. A query with fifty relevant results does not outweigh a query with one, and zero-relevance queries are excluded.
cards.formula: MAP = arithmetic mean of AP over queries with R > 0

cards.concept: When is MAP a poor product objective?
cards.intuition: MAP assumes binary relevance and can reward improvements deeper than users ever inspect. A product exposing five results may gain no value from better ranks 20 through 50.
cards.formula: evaluation depth and relevance model must match product use

cards.intuition: For a single-answer task, score how quickly the first useful result arrives. The reciprocal makes rank 1 to 2 a large loss while making deep-rank differences small.
cards.formula: RR = 1 / first relevant rank, or 0 if none; MRR = mean RR

cards.concept: Why can MRR not be converted to average rank?
cards.intuition: Averaging reciprocals and then inverting is not the same as averaging ranks. The nonlinear reciprocal bends the distribution, so report median first-hit rank separately.
With exactly one relevant document at rank r, AP has one precision term: one relevant result among r seen. That is exactly 1/r.
After the first relevant hit, every remaining result is invisible to MRR. It fits known-item and single-answer tasks, not discovery, candidate recall, or multi-chunk RAG.
cards.formula: MRR depends only on the first relevant rank
